Outcomes and experiences of Indigenous patients in Newfoundland and Labrador’s bariatric surgery program: a pilot study

Background: Indigenous Peoples in Canada have higher obesity rates (30%–51%) than non-Indigenous populations (12%–31%), and the Truth and Reconciliation Commission of Canada (TRC) has called for expanded health research to address dis­ parities between Indigenous and non-Indigenous communities. We sought to com­ pare bariatric surgery outcomes and patient experiences in Newfoundland and Labra­ dor’s bariatric surgery program among Indigenous versus non-Indigenous patients.

Methods: We conducted a mixed-methods retrospective cohort study, including patients who underwent bariatric surgery in the province’s bariatric surgery program between 2011 and 2022. We assessed metabolic outcomes through chart review and captured patient experiences with phone survey questionnaires.

Results: Among the 30 included patients (8 Indigenous, 22 non-Indigenous), there were no significant differences in excess weight loss (45% v. 48%, p = 0.4), reduction in body mass index (9.5 v. 11.3, p = 0.2), comorbidity improvement (63% v. 73%, p = 0.6), or postoperative complications (25% v. 18%, p = 0.6) at 1 year. However, on a 1–10 Likert scale, Indigenous patients reported lower satisfaction with weight loss (6.3 v. 8.2, p = 0.03) and were less likely to recommend the program (5.6 v. 8.8, p = 0.04). Both groups cited similar challenges with program referral, transportation, and postoperative supports, and recommended a longer follow-up period and increased mental health counselling services.

Conclusion: As a response to TRC’s Calls to Action, our study shows bariatric sur­ gery outcomes in Newfoundland and Labrador were similar for Indigenous and non- Indigenous patients. Given their lower satisfaction with postoperative decrease in weight, Indigenous patients may benefit from being offered metabolic procedures with greater expected weight loss, such as Roux-en-Y gastric bypass and duodenal switch.

Contexte  : Au Canada, les peuples autochtones ont un taux d’obésité plus élevé (30 %–51 %) que les populations non autochtones (12 %–31 %), et la Commission de vérité et réconciliation (CVR) du Canada a réclamé que soit menée une recherche élargie sur les disparités en matière de santé entre les communautés autochtones et non autochtones. Nous avons voulu comparer les résultats de la chirurgie bariatrique et l’expérience des patientes et patients suivis par le Programme de chirurgie ­bariatrique de Terre-Neuve-et-Labrador (TNL) selon leur appartenance ou non à un peuple autochtone.

Méthodes : Nous avons procédé à une étude de cohorte rétrospective à méthodes mixtes regroupant des personnes soumises à une chirurgie bariatrique dans le cadre du programme de chirurgie bariatrique de TNL entre 2011 et 2022. Nous avons évalué les résultats métaboliques en analysant les dossiers et recueilli l’expérience des pa­tientes et patients lors d’entrevues téléphoniques.

Résultats : Parmi les 30 personnes incluses (8 Autochtones, 22 non-Autochtones), on n’a noté aucune différence significative aux plans de la perte de poids (45 % c. 48 %, p = 0,4), de la réduction de l’indice de masse corporelle (9,5 c. 11,3, p = 0,2), de l’amélioration des comorbidités (63 % c. 73 %, p = 0.6), ou des complications post­ opératoires (25 % c. 18 %, p = 0,6) au bout de 1 an. Par contre sur une échelle de ­Likert allant de 1 à 10, les personnes autochtones se sont déclarées moins satisfaites de leur perte de poids, (6,3 c. 8,2, p = 0,03) et étaient moins susceptibles de recommander le programme (5,6 c. 8,8, p = 0,04). Les 2 groupes ont mentionné des difficultés simi­ laires relativement au programme (demande de consultation, transport et soutien postopératoire) et ont suggéré de prolonger la période de suivi et d’ajouter des ser­ vices en santé mentale.

## O

besity is a chronic disease with substantial associ­ ated morbidity and mortality, and has become a global epidemic. Other diseases such as diabetes, heart failure and other cardiovascular diseases, cirrhosis, osteoarthritis, obstructive sleep apnea, polycystic ovary disease, depression, and numerous cancers, as well as death, have been strongly associated with obesity. In Can­ ada, the prevalence of obesity has increased from less than 10% in 1985 to 30% in 2022.1 In Canada, Indigenous populations have higher rates of obesity (30%–51%) than non-­Indigenous populations (12%–31%).2,3 Social deter­ minants of health are known to contribute to Indigenous peoples’ health inequity.

The Truth and Reconciliation Commission (TRC) of Canada, as part of its Calls to Action, has recom­ mended research to close gaps in health outcomes between Indigen­ous and non-Indigenous communities.4 Previous literature has shown no difference in weight loss outcomes in Indigenous and non-Indigenous patients who have undergone bariatric surgery.6,7 How­ ever, 9.3% of Newfoundland and Labrador’s (NL) popu­ lation are Indigen­ous, higher than previously reported study populations.5–7 Given the higher Indigenous popu­lation density, as well as a response to TRC’s Calls to Action, the objective of this study was to compare bariatric surgery outcomes and patient experiences in NL’s bariatric surgery program among Indigenous and non-Indigenous patients.

## Methods

We conducted a mixed-methods retrospective cohort study. The study population consisted of patients who underwent bariatric surgery in NL’s bariatric surgery pro­ gram between January 2011 and December 2022. We included patients from consenting Indigenous commun­ ities after discussions with their respective Indigenous community leaders. We excluded patients without 1-year postoperative follow-up data and those from nonconsent­ ing Indigenous communities.

We obtained quantitative data from the patient’s electronic medical record. This included baseline demo­ graphic data (e.g., age, sex, comorbidities) and data on bariatric surgery, including type of bariatric procedure, postoperative complications, pre- and postoperative body mass index (BMI), percentage of excess body weight loss, and change in comorbidities. We obtained

data from preoperative bariatric surgery clinic notes, operative notes, inpatient progress notes, and 1-year postoperative follow-up clinic notes.

We gathered qualitative data using a 15-minute phone survey questionnaire with a focus on patient experience. The questionnaire was designed in collaboration with the NL bariatric surgery program’s surgeons, nurse practi­ tioner, and allied-health professionals, and NL’s Indigen­ ous community leaders. Questionnaire topics encom­ passed barriers to care access (e.g., referral, wait time, financial issues, transportation issues), weight loss and comorbidity resolution, patient satisfaction, postoperative supports, expectations, and other suggestions for the pro­ gram (Appendix 1, Figure 1, available at www.canjsurg.ca/ lookup/doi/10.1503/cjs.000125/tab-related-content). Ques­ tionnaires included a 10-point Likert scale and closeended and open-ended questions to bolster collected data from the surveys.

Statistical analysis

We assessed quantitative data for statistical significance, using χ2 and independent samples t tests, with a threshold p value of 0.05 as level of significance. We analyzed quali­ tative data using grounded theory to code responses and assess themes and patterns in patient experience.

Ethics approval

This study was approved by NL’s Health Research Ethics Board (no. 2022.091).

## Results

We enrolled a total of 30 patients in the study, including 8 Indigenous and 22 non-Indigenous patients. Baseline demographic characteristics with respect to age (mean 51.0 yr v. 48.0 yr, p = 0.2) and preoperative BMI (mean 47.0 v. 49.7, p = 0.2) were statistically similar between the 2 groups. However, there were more females (n = 8, 100%) in the Indigenous group than the non-Indigenous group (n = 19, 86.4%; p  =  0.04). The frequency of ­obesity-associated comorbidities of type 2 diabetes, gastro­ esophageal reflux disease (GERD), hypertension, obstruct­ ive sleep apnea, dyslipidemia, and osteoarthritis were also similar between the groups. Laparoscopic sleeve gastrec­ tomy was the most commonly performed ­procedure

Conclusion : En réponse à la demande adressée par la CVR, notre étude montre que les résultats de la chirurgie bariatrique à TNL sont similaires selon que les patientes et patients sont ou non d’origine autochtone. Compte tenu du degré moindre de satis­ faction des personnes autochtones à l’égard de la perte de poids après l’intervention, elles gagneraient peut-être à se voir offrir des modalités métaboliques permettant une plus grande perte de poids, comme la dérivation gastrique Roux-en-Y et la dérivation biliopancréatique avec commutation duodénale.

The other procedures were laparo­ scopic sleeve gastrectomy converted to open sleeve gas­ trectomy (12.5% among Indigenous patients, 4.5% among non-Indigenous patients) and laparoscopic reversal of ­vertical-banded gastroplasty (12.5% among Indigenous patients, 0% among non-Indigenous patients) (Table 1).

Metabolic outcomes

There were no differences in weight loss outcomes after bariatric surgery between the Indigenous and non- Indigenous groups at 1-year follow-up (percentage of excess body weight loss 44.8% v. 47.9%, p  =  0.4; change in BMI –9.5 v. –11.3, p  =  0.2). Postoperative complications between the groups were also similar (n = 2, 25.0% v. n = 4, 18.2%; p = 0.7). Complications included GERD (n = 0, 0.0% v. n = 2, 9.1%; p = 0.4), wound infection (n = 1, 12.5% v. n = 0, 0.0%; p = 0.09), paraesophageal hernia (n  =  1, 12.5% v. n  = 0, 0.0%; p  =  0.09), and pulmonary embolism (n  =  0, 0.0% v. n = 1, 4.5%; p = 0.5). Moreover, there were no differ­ ences in the number of patients with postoperative improvement in comorbidities between the Indigenous and non-Indigenous groups (n  =  5, 62.5% v. n  = 16, 72.7%; p = 0.6) or the number of improved comorbid­ ities per patient (0.9 v. 1.2, p = 0.2). Improvements were similar for type 2 diabetes (n  =  1, 12.5% v. n  =  9, 40.9%; p = 0.1), hypertension (n = 3, 37.5% v. n = 8, 36.4%; p  =  0.95), dyslipidemia (n = 0, 0.0% v. n = 5, 22.7%; p  =  0.1), and obstructive sleep apnea (n  =  1, 12.5% v. n  =  4, 18.2%; p  =  0.7), but the Indigenous group showed more improvement for GERD (n  =  2, 25.0% v. n = 0, 0.0%; p = 0.02) (Table 2).

Experiences with the bariatric surgery program

On a 1–10 Likert scale, Indigenous patients were less satis­fied with their weight loss (6.3 v. 8.2, p = 0.03) and less likely to refer a community member to the bariatric surgery program (5.6 v. 8.8, p  =  0.04) than non-­ Indigenous patients. Both groups had similar ratings on difficulty being referred to the program (5.5 v. 3.2, p = 0.06), transportation accessibility (6.6 v. 5.9, p = 0.3), post­operative support availability (6.5 v. 7.5, p = 0.2), and overall experience with the program (7.3 v. 8.6, p = 0.08). Financial accessibility to the bariatric surgery program was better rated by the Indigenous group (9.2 v. 7.1, p < 0.01) (Table 3).

Other pre- and postoperative experiences were statis­ tically similar between the Indigenous and non-­ Indigenous patients. Most patients were able to undergo bariatric surgery within 6 months to 1 year (n = 3, 37.5% v. n = 7, 31.8%; p = 0.8) or 1–2 years (n = 3, 37.5% v. n = 9, 40.9%; p = 0.9) of referral. Both groups suggested the need for longer patient follow-up than 18 months (n = 3, 37.5% v. n = 8, 36.4%; p = 0.95) and the need for more mental health services (n  =  1, 12.5% v. n  =  9, 40.9%; p = 0.1), more dietitian counselling (n = 1, 12.5% v. n = 3, 13.6%; p = 0.9) and a postoperative cosmesis education program (n = 2, 25.0% v. n = 1, 4.5%; p = 0.1). The most common source of initial information about the program came from friends and family (n = 5, 62.5% v. n = 9, 40.9%; p = 0.3), with family physicians and nurse practitioners providing most referrals (n = 7, 87.5% v. n = 19, 86.4%; p = 0.9). The most commonly available and used postoperative support person was the bariatric program nurse practitioner (n = 4, 50.0% v. n = 8, 36.4%; p = 0.5). Factors contributing to weight regain included lack of motivation (n = 2, 25.0% v. n = 8, 36.4%; p = 0.6) and insufficient support from the bariatric team (n = 2, 25.0% v. n = 7, 31.8%; p = 0.7). ## Discussion

In NL, a region with a high density of Indigenous people, our study demonstrated that weight loss outcomes after bariatric surgery were similar among Indigenous and non-Indigenous patients, in keeping with previous find­ ings.6–8 Postoperative complication rates were also similar between the 2 groups. Baseline preoperative BMI and comorbidities were similar between our 2 study groups.2 Improvement in these comorbidities was similar across both populations. These results suggest bariatric surgery to be equally as effective and beneficial to Indigenous and non-Indigenous patients. In Canada, with the general Indigenous population having higher obesity rates than the non-Indigenous population, this is a particularly important finding.

The perioperative experiences with the bariatric sur­ gery program were similar among Indigenous and non-

Indigenous patients, with a few notable differences. First, Indigenous patients were less satisfied with their weight loss than non-Indigenous patients, even though both groups had similar preoperative BMI and post­ operative decrease in BMI. Most patients in the study underwent laparoscopic sleeve gastrectomy, and it is possible that the Indigenous population hoped to lose more weight than what this procedure offers. Laparo­ scopic sleeve gastrectomy is known to result in an excess body weight loss of 60% at 2 years, whereas other standard bariatric procedures such as laparoscopic Roux-en-Y gastric bypass and duodenal switch result in 70% and 80% excess body weight loss in 2 years, respectively.9 The novel endoscopic sleeve gastroplasty results in less weight loss than sleeve gastrectomy, with 25% excess body weight loss in 2 years.10 In keeping with being the most performed bariatric surgery pro­ cedure worldwide, NL’s bariatric surgery program per­ forms laparoscopic sleeve gastrectomy as the procedure of choice.10 However, for Indigenous patients seeking more substantial weight loss, collaborative discussions regarding the use of more effective weight loss proced­ ures, such as Roux-en-Y gastric bypass and duodenal switch, should take place. This may not only improve their satisfaction levels, but may also make this popula­ tion more likely to refer others in their com­munity. Satisfaction with the bariatric team may also be improved by increasing the frequency and length of follow­-up. Lastly, Indigenous patients reported better financial accessibility for the bariatric surgery program. This may in part be owing to numerous federal and provincial funding programs aimed at improving In­digenous health care.12,13

Limitations

Our sample size was small, given the relatively modest number of bariatric surgeries performed annually in NL,14 our inability to get in touch with many of the Indigenous patients to consent for the study, and the fact that some Indigenous communities declined to participate in the study. We respected these patients’ and communities’ deci­ sions and suggest future studies replicate this study model in other regions with large Indigenous populations to strengthen the findings. Our study did not distinguish between Indigen­ous patients who lived on or off reserve. Future studies can explore this topic to see if there are dif­ ferences in access to care and in clinical outcomes and experiences with bariatric surgery. Another limitation was the lack of study patients undergoing laparoscopic Rouxen-Y gastric bypass, the second most common bariatric procedure worldwide. These patients are at risk of compli­ cations not seen with sleeve gastrec­tomy and that require urgent bariatric care, including marginal ulcers and inter­ nal hernias.15 Subsequent studies should include bariatric surgery programs that perform Roux-en-Y gastric bypasses to assess Indigenous patients’ care and experiences of these specific complications.

## Conclusion

Our study responds to the TRC’s Calls to Action and demonstrates that bariatric surgery outcomes are similar between Indigenous and non-Indigenous patients. Experi­ ences with the bariatric program were similar between groups, but there is an opportunity to improve patient satis­faction with weight loss and postoperative supports for Indigenous patients. Future studies should expand on this pilot study to include other regions with a high dens­ ity of Indigenous people to strengthen the findings.
